title: GMAT Focus Data Insights Practice Test 2
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt:
A bar chart shows parcels delivered last week and the number of vans at each depot:

Ashby: 9,200 parcels, 24 vans
Brent: 14,100 parcels, 39 vans
Calder: 6,800 parcels, 15 vans
Dunham: 11,500 parcels, 33 vans
Ewell: 8,400 parcels, 19 vans

Which depot delivered the most parcels per van?
questions.explanation: Parcels divided by vans: Ashby 383, Brent 362, Calder 453, Dunham 348, Ewell 442. Calder is highest at about 453 per van. The depot delivering the most parcels in total has more vans and is not the most productive per van.

questions.prompt:
Annual revenue for a manufacturer, in millions:

2021: 8.40
2022: 7.98
2023: 8.55
2024: 7.35
2025: 7.20

In which year was the percentage fall from the previous year the largest?
options: E. Revenue did not fall in any year
questions.explanation: Year-on-year change: 2022 -5.0%, 2023 +7.1%, 2024 -14.0%, 2025 -2.0%. The largest fall is 2024 at -14.0%. 2025 falls by a smaller amount and a smaller percentage, and 2023 rises.

questions.prompt:
A stacked bar shows the share of a retailer's revenue by line:

Handsets: 41%
Accessories: 18%
Airtime: 22%
Insurance: 11%
Repairs: 8%

What is the smallest number of lines that together account for at least 75% of revenue?
options: E. The threshold cannot be reached
questions.explanation: Largest first: 41% + 22% = 63%, short of 75. Adding Accessories reaches 81%. So 3 lines are needed.

questions.prompt:
Two offices of the same firm:

Northgate: 48 staff, mean salary GBP 31,200.00
Southgate: 22 staff, mean salary GBP 38,400.00

What is the mean salary across all staff in the two offices combined?
questions.explanation: The combined mean must be weighted by headcount, not averaged: total pay is Northgate 48 × GBP 31,200.00 plus Southgate 22 × GBP 38,400.00 = GBP 2,342,400.00, over 70 staff, giving GBP 33,463.00. The unweighted average of the two figures, GBP 34,800.00, is the trap and is too high because the better-paid office is the smaller one.

questions.prompt:
A van can be hired on either of two terms:

Option A: GBP 45.00 a day plus GBP 0.22 a mile
Option B: GBP 70.00 a day plus GBP 0.11 a mile

Select the mileage at which the two options cost the same for one day, AND the cheaper option for a 150-mile day.
options: A. 227 miles; Option B is cheaper at 150 miles
B. 200 miles; Option A is cheaper at 150 miles
C. 227 miles; Option A is cheaper at 150 miles
D. 300 miles; Option B is cheaper at 150 miles
E. The two options never cost the same
questions.explanation: They are equal when 45 + 0.22m = 70 + 0.11m, so m = 25 / 0.11 = 227 miles. At 150 miles: A costs GBP 78.00 and B costs GBP 86.50, so Option A is cheaper — below the crossover the lower daily rate wins.

questions.prompt:
Three suppliers quote a unit price, with a bulk discount applying only to orders of 500 units or more:

Supplier K: GBP 2.40 per unit, bulk discount 0%
Supplier M: GBP 2.95 per unit, bulk discount 12%
Supplier N: GBP 3.30 per unit, bulk discount 25%

Select the cheapest supplier for an order of 300 units AND the cheapest for an order of 1,200 units.
options: A. Supplier K at 300; Supplier K at 1,200
B. Supplier K at 300; Supplier M at 1,200
C. Supplier M at 300; Supplier N at 1,200
D. Supplier N at 300; Supplier K at 1,200
E. Supplier M at 300; Supplier M at 1,200
questions.explanation: At 300 units no discount applies, so the lowest list price wins: Supplier K GBP 720.00, Supplier M GBP 885.00, Supplier N GBP 990.00. At 1,200 units the discounts apply: Supplier K GBP 2,880.00, Supplier M GBP 3,115.20, Supplier N GBP 2,970.00. The discount is not large enough to overturn the price ranking, which is why the same supplier wins twice.

questions.prompt:
A market stall pays GBP 3,200.00 a season for its pitch. Each item sells for GBP 26.00 and costs GBP 14.00 to buy in.

Select the number of items that must be sold to break even AND the profit if 400 items are sold.
questions.explanation: Contribution per item is GBP 26.00 minus GBP 14.00 = GBP 12.00. Break-even is GBP 3,200.00 / GBP 12.00 = 267 items. At 400 items, contribution is GBP 4,800.00, less the GBP 3,200.00 pitch, leaving GBP 1,600.00.

questions.prompt:
Two savings schemes, each starting from GBP 5,000.00 with interest compounded annually:

Scheme P: 6.0% a year
Scheme Q: 4.5% a year

Select the value of Scheme P after ten years AND the amount by which it exceeds Scheme Q at that point.
questions.explanation: Compounding, not simple interest: 5,000 × 1.06^10 = GBP 8,954.24, against 5,000 × 1.045^10 = GBP 7,764.85, a difference of GBP 1,189.39. Simple interest would give GBP 8,000.00, which is the distractor.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (memo): "Central uses far more energy than any other site and should be the focus of the efficiency programme."

SOURCE 2 (table): floor area in square metres — Riverside 4,200, Parkway 2,600, Central 5,100

SOURCE 3 (table): annual energy use in kWh — Riverside 96,000, Parkway 52,000, Central 143,000

Which site uses the most energy per square metre?
options: C. All three are equal per square metre
D. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: Energy per square metre: Riverside 22.9, Parkway 20.0, Central 28.0. Central is highest. Central uses the most energy in total, which is what the memo notices, but it is also the largest building.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (screening report): "The test identifies 98% of faulty units correctly, and wrongly flags only 3% of sound units."

SOURCE 2 (production data): "Of 10,000 units produced, 200 are faulty."

SOURCE 3 (email): "We plan to scrap every unit the test flags."

Approximately what proportion of the units scrapped under that plan would actually be sound?
questions.explanation: Of 200 faulty units the test flags 196. Of 9,800 sound units it wrongly flags 3%, which is 294. Total flagged is 490, of which 294 are sound — about 60%. A test that is accurate on both measures still condemns mostly sound units when the fault rate is low, which is the base-rate point Source 2 supplies and Source 1 alone conceals.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): shipments handled this quarter — Carrier V 3,200, Carrier W 900, Carrier X 5,400

SOURCE 2 (table): late-delivery rate — Carrier V 4.5%, Carrier W 11%, Carrier X 2.8%

SOURCE 3 (email): "Compensation is paid per late delivery, so we want to reduce the total number of late deliveries."

Which carrier accounts for the greatest number of late deliveries?
options: D. The three carriers are equal
E. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: Late deliveries are shipments multiplied by the rate: Carrier V 144, Carrier W 99, Carrier X 151. Carrier X is highest. Carrier W has by far the worst rate but handles too few shipments to dominate the total, which is the distinction Source 3 makes relevant.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (memo): "Since we introduced the loyalty card, average spend per transaction has risen from GBP 18.40 to GBP 21.10."

SOURCE 2 (table): transactions per week fell from 12,400 to 10,050 over the same period.

SOURCE 3 (email): "Only card holders may use the express tills."

Which statement is best supported?
options: A. Weekly revenue rose, because average spend rose
B. Weekly revenue fell, because the drop in transactions outweighs the rise in average spend
D. The loyalty card caused the fall in transactions
E. No conclusion about revenue is possible from these sources
questions.explanation: Revenue is spend multiplied by transactions: before, GBP 18.40 × 12,400 = GBP 228,160.00; after, GBP 21.10 × 10,050 = GBP 212,055.00 — a fall. Option D asserts causation the sources do not establish, and Source 1 alone supports option A, which is why the table matters.

questions.prompt:
A team of five people has a mean age of 34. What is the age of the oldest member?

(1) The four youngest members have a mean age of 30.
(2) The youngest member is 26.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: The five ages total 5 × 34 = 170. From (1) the four youngest total 4 × 30 = 120, so the oldest is 50 — sufficient. From (2) knowing one member is 26 leaves the remaining 144 distributed in many ways — insufficient.

questions.prompt:
A shop's takings rose from June to July. By what percentage did they rise?

(1) July takings were GBP 6,900.00.
(2) Takings rose by GBP 900.00.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: Neither alone fixes both endpoints. Together, June was 6,900 − 900 = GBP 6,000.00, so the rise is 900/6,000 = 15% — sufficient. Note that (2) alone gives the amount but not the base, which is what a percentage requires.

questions.prompt:
Is the mean of four different positive integers greater than 10?

(1) The largest of them is 19.
(2) The smallest of them is 9.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: From (1) the others could be 1, 2, 3 (mean 6.25) or 16, 17, 18 (mean 17.5) — insufficient. From (2) all four are different integers of at least 9, so the smallest possible set is 9, 10, 11, 12 with mean 10.5, and any other set is larger — sufficient.

questions.prompt:
A factory ran two shifts on Tuesday. Did the night shift produce more units than the day shift?

(1) The two shifts produced 1,860 units between them.
(2) The night shift produced 8% more units per hour than the day shift.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) gives only the total. (2) gives a rate comparison but no hours: a night shift 8% faster over four hours produces less than a day shift over ten. Together the shift lengths are still unknown, so the comparison cannot be settled.

questions.prompt:
Which store generates the highest sales per square metre of floor area?

Store | Annual sales | Floor area (sq m) | Staff | Returns rate
Ashfield | GBP 412,000.00 | 640 | 18 | 4.2%
Bexley | GBP 268,000.00 | 310 | 11 | 2.8%
Cranmore | GBP 594,000.00 | 980 | 26 | 6.1%
Dunsley | GBP 197,000.00 | 250 | 9 | 3.4%
Eastwick | GBP 351,000.00 | 430 | 15 | 1.9%
Fenwick | GBP 480,000.00 | 720 | 21 | 5.5%
questions.explanation: Sales divided by floor area: Ashfield GBP 643.75, Bexley GBP 864.52, Cranmore GBP 606.12, Dunsley GBP 788.00, Eastwick GBP 816.28, Fenwick GBP 666.67. Bexley is highest. The store with the largest total sales occupies the most space and is not the most efficient use of floor area.

questions.prompt:
How many stores have a returns rate above the mean returns rate for the six?

Store | Annual sales | Floor area (sq m) | Staff | Returns rate
Ashfield | GBP 412,000.00 | 640 | 18 | 4.2%
Bexley | GBP 268,000.00 | 310 | 11 | 2.8%
Cranmore | GBP 594,000.00 | 980 | 26 | 6.1%
Dunsley | GBP 197,000.00 | 250 | 9 | 3.4%
Eastwick | GBP 351,000.00 | 430 | 15 | 1.9%
Fenwick | GBP 480,000.00 | 720 | 21 | 5.5%
questions.explanation: The mean returns rate is (4.2 + 2.8 + 6.1 + 3.4 + 1.9 + 5.5) / 6 = 3.98%. Above it are Ashfield 4.2%, Cranmore 6.1%, Fenwick 5.5% — 3 stores.

questions.prompt:
Which store has the greatest value of goods returned in a year?

Store | Annual sales | Floor area (sq m) | Staff | Returns rate
Ashfield | GBP 412,000.00 | 640 | 18 | 4.2%
Bexley | GBP 268,000.00 | 310 | 11 | 2.8%
Cranmore | GBP 594,000.00 | 980 | 26 | 6.1%
Dunsley | GBP 197,000.00 | 250 | 9 | 3.4%
Eastwick | GBP 351,000.00 | 430 | 15 | 1.9%
Fenwick | GBP 480,000.00 | 720 | 21 | 5.5%
questions.explanation: Returned value is sales multiplied by the returns rate: Ashfield GBP 17,304.00, Bexley GBP 7,504.00, Cranmore GBP 36,234.00, Dunsley GBP 6,698.00, Eastwick GBP 6,669.00, Fenwick GBP 26,400.00. Cranmore is highest at GBP 36,234.00. It has neither the worst returns rate nor, on its own, the largest sales figure deciding the outcome.

questions.prompt:
Which store ranks third highest on sales per member of staff?

Store | Annual sales | Floor area (sq m) | Staff | Returns rate
Ashfield | GBP 412,000.00 | 640 | 18 | 4.2%
Bexley | GBP 268,000.00 | 310 | 11 | 2.8%
Cranmore | GBP 594,000.00 | 980 | 26 | 6.1%
Dunsley | GBP 197,000.00 | 250 | 9 | 3.4%
Eastwick | GBP 351,000.00 | 430 | 15 | 1.9%
Fenwick | GBP 480,000.00 | 720 | 21 | 5.5%
questions.explanation: Sales per staff member: Ashfield GBP 22,888.89, Bexley GBP 24,363.64, Cranmore GBP 22,846.15, Dunsley GBP 21,888.89, Eastwick GBP 23,400.00, Fenwick GBP 22,857.14. Ranked highest first: Bexley, Eastwick, Ashfield, Fenwick, Cranmore, Dunsley. Third is Ashfield.
